notes: Recommended. Same starting point: 2024 and 2025 reports still found no legislative developments and the 2025 report says "The government launched early preparations for developing legislative amendments that would revoke work and other restrictions for EU citizens." Foreigners Act amendments were then in force from 17 January 2026 (law firm note; annual quota exemption confirmed there, work permit point not). The EU common position of 12 June 2026 notes they remove "upon the date of accession to the EU, all restrictions based on nationality with regard to the access to the labour market for EU citizens" and that the Law on Civil Servants and State Employees gives EU nationals civil service access in line with Article 45(4) TFEU; it finds the closing benchmark fulfilled. Outcome is only partly shown: this is EU acceptance of legal alignment, and "The aligned national legislation will start to apply by the date of Montenegro's accession", so no effect in practice can be seen yet. Adoption is not success, so reform_went is unknown. The most useful lesson is sequencing: fast legislation, deferred application. Caution: the common position is marked LIMITE though served openly on the Council register; the analyst should decide whether it may be registered and quoted. No independent assessment found.

Recommended, the only comparator where removal has been applied. Timing: the 2007 screening report records EU workers under conditions "the same as those applying to nationals of third countries" with amendments in preparation to abolish permits for EU nationals (working group from April 2005). The 2009 and 2011 reports say Croatia "largely" fulfils the requirements; SWD(2012) 338, nine months before accession on 1 July 2013, says "Croatia has completed alignment with the acquis". COM(2015) 233 then shows an applied consequence: "Croatia decided to introduce reciprocal restrictions for workers from these Member States and requires a work permit from their nationals", for the 13 restricting states, so removal was not complete on accession day. Mixed because the public sector point is unresolved: the 2007 report planned limits on civil servant posts, and a Croatian law school paper seen only as a search snippet (repository returned a robot check, not bypassed) says a citizenship certificate left EU nationals with free access only to private employment or self-employment. I could not confirm this from the Civil Servants Act or the network report. Limits: all evidence pre-dates 2020 so needs a logged exception; no data found on EU workers actually entering Croatia; COM(2015) 233 and the wiiw study concern Croatians moving out; the Aliens Act text was reached only as a contents page. Very different country context and reforms made in an earlier period.

Recommended as the stalled case and closest wording match to North Macedonia. 2021, 2024 and 2025 reports all say EU citizens are "covered by rules for third-country nationals" (2025: "the legislative framework is partially aligned with the EU acquis as EU citizens are currently covered by rules for third-country nationals"). Screening report: under the 2014 Law on Employment of Foreigners "Free access to the Serbian labour market will be provided for EU citizens" and "These provisions will enter into force on the date of accession"; for civil servant posts "Serbian citizenship/nationality is required, except for the health sector". Yet the 2025 report asks Serbia to "start preparing for the alignment of national legislation with the EU acquis on free movement of workers". Reforms since (2020 and 2023 amendments, single permit from 2024) simplified procedures for foreigners generally without creating an EU regime. Permit data exist: more than 2 300 to EU citizens in 2020, 2 071 in 2023, 526 (3%) in 2024, but the totals moved sharply (about 13 000, 50 397, 17 251), probably from a counting or system change, so do not read them as a trend without checking. Whether the accession clause remains in the current law was not confirmed. No independent outcome assessment found; WB6 study is about posted workers.

Not recommended. Only partly the same issue, because Albania already separates EU citizens; the shared part is the public post reservation: "Employment in civil service positions and in the state police require Albanian citizenship" (2024 and 2025 reports, unchanged). The 2025 amendments (Article 33/1, per law firm note) recognise a right to move, reside and work without tying it to accession, which is a contrast with the deferred model, but no assessment of how they work was found. Evidence conflicts on whether EU citizens need permits: the WB6 study and PwC say exempt, while the 2025 report says 1 314 of 11 224 work permits "were granted to EU citizens" and also describes a simplified procedure. This should be reported rather than resolved. Fails the need for a close match with the North Macedonian starting point.

Close call, not recommended; first reserve. Good issue match and an active reform: January 2024 amendments "allow EU citizens (and a number of other countries) to work in Moldova without a work permit"; July 2025 law "providing for a different regime for EU citizens wishing to work in Moldova, than other third country nationals"; Law 200/2025 in force 18 March 2026 (press report). But "EU citizens still have no access to posts in public administration bodies" and the 2025 report still asks Moldova to "align national legislation with the EU acquis on access for EU citizens to the labour market". The law came into force after the latest Commission report, so nothing assesses its effect; preparation level moved from early stage (2024) to some level (2025), and the rating covers the whole chapter. Law text not reached; whether it applies before accession is not confirmed. Would replace Serbia if the analyst prefers an early application model over a stalled case.
